Because all subclasses inherit the Object class by default, all subclasses can call the equals() method in the Object class. Therefore, it is convenient to use the equals method directly to compare whether two objects have the same reference in a subclass, which is an advantage. In addition, in some subclasses, such as String, this class overrides the equals() method in the Object class. entry.content:
Questions

When should you consider using recursive algorithms when writing a program? Discuss in terms of advantages and disadvantages.

1. Definition of recursion

“A recursive method is a method that calls itself” (Seiter & Palmer, 2019). A recursive method usually consists of two parts: one is the base case, which halts the recursion; the other is the recursive call, that is, calling the method itself inside the method. “Every recursive method must have at least one base case” (Seiter & Palmer, 2019). If a recursive method has no base case, then the recursion is called infinite recursion. This method will call itself repeatedly until the program eventually crashes.

For example, in the above program, the printHello() method calls itself internally, so printHello() is a recursive method. However, since this recursive method lacks a base case, it is called infinite recursion. Due to the lack of a base case to stop the recursion, the printHello() will crash with a StackOverflowError.

2. Scenarios suitable for using recursive algorithms

“Recursion is most useful when it is used to solve problems where the structure of the problem repeats” (Seiter & Palmer, 2019). For example, we can use recursion to calculate Fibonacci numbers, which is defined by the recurrence relation: f0 =0; f1 =1; fn = fn-1 + f n-2, for n>1.

According to Seiter & Palmer, “any recursive solution could be written with iteration (loops) instead” (2019). So, in what scenarios is recursion used, and what problems are suitable for iteration? Generally speaking, “iteration is usually preferred and more efficient, but recursive solutions can be elegant and require less code” (Downey & Mayfield, 2019, p. 127).

To further illustrate when recursive algorithms should be considered when writing programs, I will give an example that uses recursion and iteration to calculate Fibonacci numbers. Then, I will illustrate the recursion‘s pros and cons by comparing the two algorithms’ code size and time complexity.

Codes:

In the above example, the pros and cons of using recursion are clear. On the one hand, we can see that the recursive method recursiveFibonacci() is more concise than the iterative method iterativeFibonacci(). In other words, recursiveFibonacci() has less code than iterative Fibonacci(). This is the advantage of recursion. On the other hand, when calculating the Fibonacci number f(20), recursion takes 424100 ns, and iteration takes 2500 ns. Therefore, recursion requires more time than iteration in this case, which is “because the call stack is so heavily used during recursion” (Stack Overflow, n.d.). This is the disadvantage of recursion.

3. In Conclusion

In general, recursion is more elegant and requires less code than iteration, but in some cases, it may take longer to run because recursion requires a lot of call stacks. Hence, if we seek code simplicity, recursion may be a better choice than iteration; if we pursue a faster running time, iteration may be better than recursion.

CS1103 Learning Journal Unit 3 - ADTs, Stacks, Queues and Binary Trees

This week, I learned about abstract data type (ADT), stacks, queues, and binary trees. Firstly, ADT “refers to a set of possible values and a set of operations on those values, without any specification of how the values are to be represented or how the operations are to be implemented” (Eck, 2019, p. 450). In this case, “a program that only depends on the abstract definition of the ADT can use either implementation, interchangeably” (UoPeople, n.d.), which is helpful to debug and maintain. Secondly, the stack is a common abstract data type, and it has three methods: push(), pop(), and isEmpty(). We can use several ways to implement a stack, such as a linked list and an array. Thirdly, the queue is another common abstract data type, and it has three methods: enqueue(), dequeue(), and isEmpty(). A queue can also be implemented by a linked list or an array. Fourthly, “a binary tree is a tree data structure in which each node has at most two children” (UoPeople, n.d.). We can traverse a binary tree in three orders: preorder traversal, postorder traversal, and inorder traversal.

Finally, generics and wrapper classes mean that Java generic programming is unsuitable for primitive data types. Still, we can use wrapper classes to convert primitive data types to wrapper types and then handle these wrapper types by generic programming.

In the discussion forum, I detailed the advantages and disadvantages of the equals() method and the alternative for equality. First, the equals() method is a method of the Object class, and all subclasses of the Object class inherit this method by default. The equals() method has advantages and disadvantages. On the one hand, the advantage of this method is that it can easily compare whether the references of two objects are the same, and some methods, such as String, override the equals() method by default, so one can use it directly to compare the content of the two strings. On the other hand, the disadvantage of the equals() method is that not all subclasses override the equals() method by default. In this case, the equals() method can only compare the reference of the object, not the content. If one needs to compare the contents, he/she needs to override the equals() method. Additionally, there are many alternatives to the equals() method, such as the ‘==’, compareTo() and compare() methods. I detailed the compareTo() method with an example in the discussion assignment.

entry.title: CS2401 Discussion Assignment Unit 1 - The Difference between Developing an Aircraft, a Bridge and a Word Processor
entry.content:
Question

A passenger aircraft is composed of several millions of parts and requires thousands of persons to assemble. A four-lane highway bridge is another example of complexity. The first version of Word for Windows, a word processor released by Microsoft in 1989, required 55 person-years, resulted into 249,000 lines of source code, and was delivered 4 years late. Aircraft and highway bridges are usually delivered on time and within budget, whereas software is often not. Discuss what are, in your opinion, the differences between developing an aircraft, a bridge, and a word processor that would cause this situation.

Answers

Software engineering development is to solve problems in the real world, such as writing a word processor, including design, implementation, and testing (Marsic, 2012). Similarly, the development of physical engineering is to build a thing, such as a bridge, including design, implementation, and engineering acceptance. However, the two have some differences, and the specific content is as follows:

First, the scope of knowledge that developers need to master is different. Specifically, for the development of physical engineering, such as building a bridge, engineers only need to grasp bridge knowledge (Marsic, 2012). On the contrary, software development requires developers to understand both the problem domain and the software domain (Marsic, 2012). In other words, developers need to know the problems to be solved clearly and what kind of software technology to use to develop the corresponding products.

Second, developers have different understandings of the problem. Specifically, there will be clear drawings and accurate budgets before the physical engineering developers build an object. For example, when engineers build a bridge, they will design drawings and complete the bridge’s construction according to them. However, when software developers face a realistic problem, they usually only know approximately what to do initially (Marsic, 2012). In this case, they propose a preliminary solution and then iterate and update the software according to user feedback to develop satisfactory products.

Third, the development process is different. Specifically, engineers usually develop physical engineering with specific steps and clear standards. On the contrary, the original plan proposed by software engineering developers often only approximates actual problems (Marsic, 2012). In other words, they will develop a prototype and continue improving the software according to the user’s feedback. For example, Agile Software Development (ASD) is such a method, which will first develop a software prototype based on some understanding of the problem and then develop new versions based on the user’s feedback (Marsic, 2012).

In conclusion, the difference between software engineering and physical engineering development mainly includes three aspects. First, software developers must master the problem and software domain, and physical developers only need to master the program domain. Second, software development schemes only approximate actual problems, and physical engineering development has a clear and specific solution. Finally, the software development process is generally incremental and iterative, and the development process of physical engineering is gradually implemented according to the plan.

Specifically, plan-driven methods have detailed specifications and design before implementation, including the Waterfall Model, V-Model, and Spiral Model (Halvorsen, 2013). On the contrary, agile methods are incremental and iterative. In other words, it needs to get feedback from users quickly to adjust the development process. entry.title: CS2401 Discussion Assignment Unit 2 - Strengths and Weaknesses of Users and Developers in Requirements Elicitation Activities
entry.content:
Questions

From your point of view, describe the strengths and weaknesses of users during the requirements elicitation activity. Describe also the strengths and weaknesses of developers during the requirements elicitation activity.

Requirements elicitation is communicating with stakeholders in the software development process to determine the requirements to be developed. It consists of four steps: requirements gathering, organizing requirements, negotiation and discussion, and documentation. In the requirement elicitation process, users and developers have strengths and weaknesses, which I will elaborate on in the next paragraphs.

Figure 1: “Requirement Elicitation Process” (TutorialsPoint, n.d., para. 7)

1. The users’ strengths and weaknesses in requirements elicitation activities

Strengths: In the requirements elicitation activities, users’ strengths are that they can clearly judge whether the requirement is what they need. Specifically, when a requirement is put forward, users can evaluate whether the requirement is what they expected so that the development team can adjust the development process according to the users’ feedback. For example, the agile development method takes full advantage of this strength of the user. In other words, the developer iteratively updates the software through interaction with the user.

Weaknesses: In the requirements elicitation activities, users’ weaknesses are that they cannot tell developers what they expect from the system to be developed (Marsic, 2012). Specifically, it is easy to suggest improvements to a system that has been created. Still, it is somewhat challenging to propose requirements for a system that has not been developed, just like getting people to change how they do business online before the invention of the Internet (Marsic, 2012).

2. The developers’ strengths and weaknesses in requirements elicitation activities

Strengths: In the requirements elicitation activities, developers’ strengths are that they can choose the right technology to realize the users’ needs after knowing them (Marsic, 2012). Specifically, developers usually have a good understanding of the technologies in the computer field, and they can pick the appropriate technology to implement requirements economically and efficiently.

Weaknesses: In the requirements elicitation activities, developers’ weaknesses are that they usually have insufficient knowledge of some specific domain (Marsic, 2012). Specifically, domain experts often use some terminology to describe problems in their domain. Still, for developers unfamiliar with this field, it is difficult to understand and master this jargon, thus hindering developers from obtaining requirements (Marsic, 2012).

In conclusion, when gathering requirements, users can judge the suitability of the requirements well but cannot clearly express the expected needs. Instead, developers can choose the appropriate computer technology according to the requirements but may lack domain knowledge.

Questions

Consider the following nonfunctional requirements and determine which of them can be verified and which cannot. Write acceptance tests for each requirement or explain why it is not testable.
a. “The user interface must be user-friendly and easy to use.”
b. “The number of mouse clicks the user needs to perform when navigating to any window of the system’s user interface must be less than 10.”
c. “The user interface of the new system must be simple enough so that any user can use it with a minimum training.”
d. “The maximum latency from the moment the user clicks a hyperlink in a web page until the rendering of the new web page starts is 1 second over a broadband connection.”
e. “In case of failure, the system must be easy to recover and must suffer minimum loss of important data.”

Answers

Acceptance tests specify situations in which user requirements may and may not work. However, the prerequisite for writing acceptance tests for a requirement is that the requirement is testable (Marsic, 2012). In other words, the requirement cannot be subjective or vague. Instead, it needs to be specific and measurable. In the following paragraphs, I’ll explain whether the requirements are testable and the corresponding reasons.

a. “The user interface must be user-friendly and easy to use.”

The requirement cannot be verified because it is ambiguous. Specifically, “user-friendly” and “easy to use” are both subjective and vague expressions, which makes testers unable to determine what kind of user interface can be considered “user-friendly” and “easy to use”. Therefore, this requirement is untestable.

b. “The number of mouse clicks the user needs to perform when navigating to any window of the system’s user interface must be less than 10.”

The requirement can be verified because less than 10 clicks are specific and measurable. Its acceptance test is as follows:

c. “The user interface of the new system must be simple enough so that any user can use it with a minimum training.”

The requirement cannot be verified because it is vague. Precisely, “simple enough” and “minimum training” are subjective descriptions, and the testers cannot make specific measurements. Therefore, this requirement is not testable.

d. “The maximum latency from the moment the user clicks a hyperlink in a web page until the rendering of the new web page starts is 1 second over a broadband connection.”

Specifically, “easy to recover”, “minimum loss”, and “important data” are all subjective expressions, and testers have no specific standards to judge what the minimum loss is, which data is essential, and whether the system is easy to recover. You are encouraged to run the SimplePaint program for yourself to test its behavior. Then read through the program carefully to understand how that behavior arises.

1. Overview of the SimplePaint.java

To create a JavaFX program, the SimplePaint class extends the abstract class Application and overrides the abstract method start() in it. In the overridden start() method, the author creates a root node as the container and a canvas node inside it. The scene graph is as follows:

To respond to the mouse operations, including mouse pressed, mouse dragged and mouse released, the author uses three lambda expressions to create three corresponding listeners, namely mouse pressed listener, mouse dragged listener, and the mouse released listener, and then he registers these listeners to the mouse event source. Hence, when the mouse event occurs, the mouse event source will automatically send the event object to the registered listener, and the listener object will call the corresponding method to process the event.

2. Details of the Mouse Event Handling

2.1. Explanation of the Event Handling Methods

Mouse Pressed: The author defines a mousePressed() method to handle the mouse pressed event. In the mousePressed(), the author uses the nested if statement to handle 3 different cases: First, the click is on the white drawing area. If so, the program will save the previous location of the mouse, set the boolean variable dragging to be true, and the width and color of the line for drawing. Second, the click is one the clear button. In this case, the program will clearAndDrawPalette() to fill the canvas with white and redraw the color palette. Third, the click is on the color palette. under this circumstance, the program will call the changeColor() method to change the drawing color.

Mouse Dragged: The author defines a mouseDragged() method to handle the mouse dragged event. In the mouseDragged(), the author uses the boolean variable dragging to determine whether the user is drawing. If the value is true, it means the user is drawing. Then, the author will adjust the coordinate of the mouse to ensure drawing on the drawing area. Finally, the author calls the strokeLine() method to draw the line.

Mouse Released: The author defines a mouseReleased() method to handle the mouse released event. In the mouseReleased(), the author set the boolean variable dragging to be false. This makes sense because the drawing stops if the mouse is released.

entry.title: CS1103 Discussion Assignment Unit 5 - Guidelines for choosing the suitable Java Collection
entry.content:
Questions

When writing a data structure, what should be our guidelines for choosing the right Java Collection?

1. Collections

Before I discuss the guidelines for choosing the right Java Collection, it is necessary to introduce concrete collections. “There are two fundamental interfaces for collections: Collection and Map” (Horstmann, 2019, p.664). Below are the classes that implement the Collection interface and Map interface.

Classes in the collections framework (Horstmann, 2019, p.667)

2. Guidelines

This part will introduce the definitions and usage scenarios of ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, Queue, Deque, PriorityQueue, Map, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap in detail.

2.1.1 List

The elements stored in the List are ordered but not necessarily in ascending or descending order. Elements can be repeated. For example [a, c, b, c].

2.1.2. ArrayList

Advantage: ArrayList can store objects except for primitive types. The number of objects that an ArrayList can store can be expanded. ArrayList supports fast random access, that is, its elements can be accessed by index.

Disadvantage: However, “ArrayList suffers from a major drawback. Removing an element from the middle of an ArrayList is expensive since all ArrayList elements beyond the removed one must be moved toward the beginning of the ArrayList. The same is true for inserting elements in the middle” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 668).

2.1.3. LinkedList

Advantage: “Removing an element from the middle of a linked list is an inexpensive operation - only the links around the element to be removed need to be updated” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 670). “The only reason to use a linked list is to minimize the cost of insertion and removal in the middle of the list” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 677).

Disadvantage: “Linked lists do not support fast random access. If you want to see the nth element of a linked list, you have to start at the beginning and skip past the first n - 1 elements. There is no shortcut. For that reason, programmers don’t usually use linked lists in situations where elements need to be accessed by an integer index” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 676).

2.1.4. Summary

(1) If we want to access elements randomly, we can use ArrayList;

(2) if we want to insert or remove elements efficiently, we can use LinkedList.

2.2.1. Set

Elements in a Set cannot be repeated and they might or might not be in some definite order (Eck, 2019).

2.2.2. HashSet

Advantage: “HashSet is a class that implements a set based on a hash table” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 685). The hash table is a data structure conducive to quickly finding elements, and HashSet is implemented based on the hash table. Hence, HashSet is suitable for situations where elements need to be quickly found.

Disadvantage: “The drawback is that the hash table gives one no control over the order in which the elements appear. Hence, one would only use a HashSet if he/she doesn’t care about the ordering of the elements in the collection” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 685).

2.2.3. LinkedHashSet

Advantage: LinkedHashSet is implemented based on linked hash table. “It can remember in which order we inserted items” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 708). Therefore, when we iterate over the elements in the LinkedHashSet with an iterator, the output order is the insertion order.

2.2.4. TreeSet

Advantage: TreeSet is a class that implements a set based on a red-black tree. “The TreeSet class is similar to the hash set, with one added improvement. A tree set is a sorted collection. We can insert elements into the collection in any order. When we iterate through the collection, the values are automatically presented in sorted order” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 687).

Disadvantage: Compared with HashSet, adding an element to TreeSet takes longer than adding an element to HashSet (Horstmann, 2019).

2.2.5. Summary

(1) If we want to find an element quickly, we can use HashSet, but when traversing, the outputs are not in a definite order;

(2) LinkedHashSet improves this shortcoming, in other words, the output order is the insertion order when traversing;

(3) TreeSet also improves this shortcoming, the output elements have a definite order, but adding elements to a TreeSet takes longer than adding elements to a HashSet.

2.3.1. Queue

A Queue is a data structure that allows adding data from the head and removing data from the tail. But we cannot add data from the middle.

2.3.2. Deque

Deque is a double-ended queue, which means we can add or remove data from the head and add or remove data from the tail.

2.3.3. PriorityQueue

“A PriorityQueue retrieves elements in sorted order after they were inserted in arbitrary order. That is, whenever we call the remove method, we get the smallest element currently in the priority queue” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 695).

2.3.4. Summary

(1) Since Queue has the characteristic of first in, first out, “Queues are typically used in a computer when only one item can be processed at a time, but several items can be waiting for processing” (Eck, 2019, p . 457). For example, when a web server processes web requests, those pending requests are stored in the Queue.

(2) PriorityQueue has some special usage scenarios because its remove() method always removes the smallest element in the current PriorityQueue. For example, a typical application of PriorityQueue is job scheduling. “Each job has a priority. Jobs are added in random order. Whenever a new job can be started, the highest priority job (priority 1) is removed from the queue” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 696).

2.4.1. Map

Advantage: Map is a data structure that stores key/value pairs. We can find the corresponding value according to the key. “A set is a collection that lets you quickly find an existing element. However, to lookup an element, you need to have an exact copy of the element to find. That isn’t a very common lookup - usually, you have some key information, and you want to look up the associated element. The map data structure serves that purpose. A map stores key/value pairs. You can find a value if you provide the key” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 697).

2.4.2. TreeMap

Advantage: “If the map is a TreeMap, then the key set of the map is a sorted set, and the iterator will visit the keys in ascending order” (Eck, 2019, p. 509).

Disadvantage: Operations on elements in TreeMap take longer than operations on elements in HashMap. For example, accessing elements in a TreeMap takes longer than accessing a HashMap.

2.4.3. HashMap

Advantage: Operations on elements in HashMap take less time than operations on elements in TreeMap. For example, accessing elements in a HashMap takes less time than accessing a TreeMap.

Disadvantage: “For a HashMap, the keys are visited in an arbitrary, unpredictable order” (Eck, 2019, p. 509).

2.4.4. LinkedHashMap:

Advantage: LinkedHashMap is an improvement of HashMap. “The LinkedHashMap classes remember in which order we inserted items” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 708). In other words, the keys are visited in insertion order.

2.4.5. Summary

entry.title: Is a default constructor always provided by the Java compiler?
entry.content:
Introduction

The Java compiler does not always provide a default constructor. It only provides a default constructor when the programmer does not provide any constructor in the class. This blog will first introduce the different types of constructors and then prove that the compiler does not always provide a default constructor.

1. Types of Constructors

Generally speaking, there are three types of constructors: the default constructor, no-parameter constructor, and constructor with parameters.

Default constructor: A constructor without parameters, which is created by the Java compiler during the compiling phase.

No-parameter constructor: A constructor without parameters, which is created by the programmers when they write the source code(.java file).

Constructor with parameters: A constructor that have some parameters, which is created by the programmers when they write the source code(.java file).

2. The Proof Process

2.1. The process of compiling and interpreting a Java program

The process of compiling and interpreting a Java program (Downey, 2019, p. 9)

The process of compiling and interpreting a Java source code is: first, a programmer writes a .java file; second, the compiler will compile it to a .class file; finally, the interpreter(JVM, Java Virtue Machine) will interpret it.

2.2. The proof steps

The Java compiler would add the default constructor when compiling the .java file into the .class file. Hence, the .class file should have a constructor created by the compiler if it did provide. Therefore, we can check the .class file to see whether the compiler would give a default constructor if the programmers do not offer any constructor. For the .class file, we can use the javap command to disassemble it, and the outputs will show us what it includes. Simply, the process is:

Compiling the .java file –> using javap to disassemble the .class file -> ckeck the outputs

Next, I will use two programs to prove: a .java file without any constructor given by the programmer and a .java file with a constructor provided by the programmer.

2.3.2. Example of a .java file with a constructor provided by the programmer

CS1103 Learning Journal Unit 6 - Files and Networking; Advanced GUI Programming

I learned about file manipulation, network communication, and advanced GUI programming this week. First, file operations include reading and writing Files. Specifically, if we want to read a file, we can use the FileReader class to create an input stream. But since the FileReader class has only some primitive methods, we can use Scanner or BufferedReader class to wrap the FileReader object; if we want to write a file, we can use the FileWriter class. Similarly, we can wrap the FileWriter object with the PrintWriter class to call its prosperous methods. In addition, one point to note is that it is a good practice to call the close() method to close the file after reading and writing it. Second, network communication mainly involves two aspects. One is to use the URL and URLConnection classes to read network resources. Concretely, we need to create a URL object first and then call the openConnection() method to get a URLConnection object, through which we can obtain the InputStream. The other is to utilize a socket to communicate between server and client. To be more specific, we need to adopt the Socket class to create a Socket object on the client-side and then use the ServerSocket class to create a ServerSocket object as the listener on the server-side. We can establish a connection between the client and the server in this case. Additionally, it is worth mentioning that before calling the close() method to end the connection, it is necessary to call the flush() method to ensure the successful sending of the data. Third, advanced GUI programming includes lots of the classes and terms: BufferedImages, Pixels, Resources, Cursors and Icons, image formats, Graphics2D Class, FontMetrics Class, Transparency, Antialiasing (UoPeople, nd), which are well used and consolidated in programming assignments.

Through the discussion assignments, I have a deeper understanding of Sockets and ServerSockets. Specifically, Socket and ServerSocket are two classes under the java.net package (UoPeople, n.d.). For the Socket class, it contains a constructor Socket(host, port), which can be used to create a Socket object to connect to a given host and port (Horstmann, 2019). For the ServerSocket class, it is used primarily on the server-side. We can use the constructor ServerSocket(port) of the ServerSocket class to create an object and monitor a port. Then we can call the accept() method to get a server socket object and establish a connection between the server and client. After transferring the data, we need to call the close() method to terminate the connection. However, before closing the connection, the flush() method needs to be called to ensure that the data was sent successfully (Eck).

In the programming assignment and exercise, I reinforce my knowledge of file manipulation. Specifically, in the programming lab, the image data needs to be saved to a text file. 1. class variables

Definition: Class variables are also called static variables. They are modified by the static modifier, belong to the class rather than objects, and can be called directly by the class name.

Application: In the Question.java file, I define two class variables: nQuestions and nCorrect, modified by the modifier static and used to count the total questions and the correct questions, respectively.

2. instance variables

Definition: Instance variables are non-static variables. They have no static modifier, belong to the object rather than class.

Application: In the Question.java file, I define two instance variables: question and correctAnswer. The difference between instance and class variables is that instance variables do not have the modifier static and belong to the object instead of the class.

3. inheritance

Definition: Inheritance means a subclass extends one superclass. The subclass will have all the methods and variables in the superclass. Besides, one subclass can only extend one superclass.

Application: The TrueFalseQuestion class and MultipleChoiceQuestion class both extend the Question class in the Quiz program. Hence, they will have all the methods and instance variables in the superclass Question. For example, the subclass TrueFalseQuestion can use the correctAnswer variable and initQuestionDialog() method, which inherit from the superclass Question.

4. polymorphism

Definition: Polymorphism means the method called at run-time depends on the actual (run-time) type instead of the declared (compile-time) type ((Seiter & Palmer, 2020). For example, the class Student extends the class People and overrides the printInfo() method. People s = new Students(); s. printInfo() will call the Student’s printInfo() method instead of the People’s. Besides, we should note that variables are not polymorphic. For instance, s.age will call the People’s variable age instead of the Student’s.

Application: The QuestionDialog class implements the ActionListener interface and overrides its actionPerformed() method. Hence, when a button is clicked, the QuestionDialog’s actionPerformed() method will be called instead of the ActionListener’s. This is polymorphism.

5. abstract classes

Definition: The abstract class is a class with the modifier abstract, it may have or not have abstract methods, and it can also include non-abstract methods. We can use a subclass to extend the abstract class but note that we cannot create objects using an abstract class directly.

Application: The class Question is an abstract class, which has a modifier abstract. And I withdraw some common features from its subclass MultipleChoiceQuestion and TrueFalseQuestion, including some variables (like correctAnswer) and some methods (like initQuestionDialog()), so the codes will be more concise.

6. “this”

Definition: The keyword this is a reference to the current object. We can use it to call other constructors (this() or this(arguments)) and distinguish an instance variable and a local parameter (this.variableName) in the same class (Seiter & Palmer, 2020).

Application: In the Question class’s constructor, I use the statement this.question = new QuestionDialog() to initialize the QuestionDialog type variable question. “this” is a reference to the current object.

7. “super”

Definition: The keyword super is a reference to the superclass object. We can use it to call the superclass constructors (super() or super(arguments)) and superclass instance methods(super.methodName) (Seiter & Palmer, 2020).

Application: In the TrueFalseQuestion class’s constructor, I use super(question) to call its superclass Question’s constructor. In the MultipleChoiceQuestion class’s constructor, I use super(query) to call its superclass Question’s constructor.

8. interfaces

Definition: An interface contains methods declaration without their implementation. To declare an interface, we need to use the keyword interface; to implement an interface, we need to use the keyword implements and override all the methods in the subclass.

Application: I use the QuestionDialog class to implement the ActionListener interface. Hence, I can create a listener to listen to the button click events, and handle it.

9. event listeners

Definition: “An event listener is an instance of a class that implements a listener
interface” ( Horstmann, 2019, p. 800).

Application: In the Question class’s construtor Question(String question), I use the statement this.question = new QuestionDialog() to initialize the variable question. The new QuestionDialog() will create an event listener object because the QuestionDialog class implements the ActionListener interface.

Introduction

In this discussion, I will first introduce the definition of MVC and then explain how Model-View-Controller (MVC) “decouples data access, business logic, data presentation, and user interaction” (UoPeople, n.d.). Next, I will use concrete code to illustrate these advantages further. Finally, I will make a summary.

1. Definition and Explanation

The Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern divides an application into three components: Model, View and Controller. Different parts have different responsibilities. Specifically, the Model is the data and the rules (business logic) for processing that data (Pastor, 2010). The view is the display interface responsible for showing the data received from the Model (Pastor, 2010). The controller is used to “coordinate interactions between the Model and View” (Banas, 2013). In other words, “it usually calls the appropriate Model for the task and then selects the proper view. It contains a lot of internal-organizational logic (more like housekeeping)” (Pastor, 2010).

Handling user requests using MVC pattern (Pastor, 2010)

I got the image above after modifying the figure from Pastor’s blog. It is beneficial for how MVC decouples user interaction, data presentation, business logic, and data access. The specific explanation is as follows: First, user interaction is in charge of the Controller. Specifically, in processes 1 and 7, when the user sends a request, the Controller will call the Model to process the data and the View to display the results. Second, data presentation is the View’s responsibility. Concretely, in steps 5 and 6, the Controller will call the appropriate View to display the data from the Model. Third, business logic is mainly handled by the Model. More specifically, as shown in processes 2 and 4, the Model will process the data according to specific rules after receiving the call request from the Controller. Fourth, data access is shown in process 3. The Model needs to read data from the database or hard disk before processing it. Based on the above explanations, we can see those different components of MVC are responsible for data access, business logic, data presentation, and user interaction, respectively. Therefore, MVC decouples these four functions nicely.

Questions

Section 6.9 of your textbook (“Debugging”) lists three possibilities to consider if a function is not working.
1.Describe each possibility in your own words.
2.Define “precondition” and “postcondition” as part of your description.
3.Create your own example of each possibility in Python code. List the code for each example, along with sample output from trying to run it.

1. Definition of the terms

A precondition is “a requirement that should be satisfied by the caller before a function starts” (Downey, 2015, p.37);

A postcondition is “a requirement that should be satisfied by the function before it ends” (Downey, 2015, p.37);

A return value is something that a function returns to the caller after it is executed. It can be None, a number, a string, a complex expression, or even a function.

2. Description of the three possibilities

When we call a function, there are three possibilities for the function’s not working:

The first case is that the preconditions are not met. Specifically, the arguments we pass to the function are incorrect, such as the arguments’ types do not match the parameters’ types or arguments’ amount mismatches the parameters’ amount, etc;

The second case is that the post-conditions are not met. Specifically, the code in the function’s body does not achieve the desired effect, maybe because the statement’s logic is incorrect, or the statements’ format is wrong, etc;

The third case is there is a problem with the return value of the function. Specifically, it may be that the function’s return value is not the value we want, or the returned value is correct, but we did not use it correctly.

But when I printed the return value, I concatenated it with an int-type number 2. Because the int-type number cannot concatenate with a string, the interpreter returned the TypeError.

In this example, the precondition and the postcondition were both met, and the return value was correct, but I misused it. So this is an example of the misuse of the return value.

4. A little story to help understand the terms and the three possibilities

4.1. Part I

Imagine you are very hungry. You go to a restaurant and order a delicious fish to relieve your hunger.

To cook a fish, the chef needs fish, salt, and oil. Providing the chef fish, salt, and oil is the precondition for cooking a fish. If the chef is given some potatoes, then the precondition is not met. If the chef does get the fish, salt, and oil, then the precondition is satisfied.

Assuming that the precondition is met, the chef also needs a recipe for cooking fish. This recipe is a postcondition. If this recipe is wrong, that is to say, according to its procedures, the chef cannot cook delicious fish, for example, the fish is scorched, then the mistake of this recipe is that the postcondition is not satisfied. If the procedure in the recipe is correct, for example, the cooking time is just right, the fish will not be scorched and will be delicious, then the postcondition is satisfied.

Assuming that both the precondition and postcondition are met, the chef has cooked a delicious fish with the right ingredients and recipe. Now, the waiter brings the fish to you. The fish served is equivalent to the return value. If the waiter brought you a bowl of soup instead of fish, the return value is wrong because you ordered a fish. If the waiter did serve a delicious fish, the return value is correct. However, If you don’t eat this fish but use it to appreciate the chef’s superb cooking skills, it misuses the return value. Because you are hungry, you need to eat the fish instead of watching it.

4.2. Part II

For programming, the fish, salt, and oil in the above story are similar to arguments, and the recipe is identical to the function. The fish served by the waiter is like the return value.

If the ingredients match the elements required by the recipe or say the arguments match the parameters, it means the precondition is met. Conversely, if the ingredients mismatch the elements required by the recipe or say the arguments mismatch the parameters, it means the precondition is not satisfied.

If the steps in the recipe are correct, and the chef can cook a delicious fish according to these steps, or say the statement in the function can achieve the effect we want, it means the postcondition is satisfied. In contrast, if the steps in the recipe are incorrect, and you can not cook a delicious fish according to these steps, or say the statement in the function can not achieve the effect we want, it means the postcondition is not satisfied.

entry.title: CS1103 Discussion Assignment Unit 1 - Who should be responsible for catching and handling exceptions: the computer or the computer program?
entry.content:
Questions

Who should be responsible for catching and handling exceptions: the computer or the computer program?

1. The Classification of Exceptions

Before discussing who is responsible for catching and handling exceptions, let’s first classify exceptions because different exceptions require different handling.

Exception hierarchy in Java (Eck, 2019, p. 403)

There are two kinds of exceptions in Java: Unchecked exceptions and checked exceptions. As shown in the above picture, the classes for unchecked exceptions are shown in blue, and the classes for checked exceptions are shown in red.

1.1. Unchecked exceptions

Unchecked exceptions: “Any exception that derives from the class Error or the class RuntimeException” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 511); “unchecked” means that these exceptions are not checked at compile-time but at runtime.

Error: “The Error hierarchy describes internal errors and resource exhaustion situations inside the Java runtime system” (Horstmann, 2019, p. 510); this kind of exception is checked at runtime.

RuntimeException: RuntimeException is usually caused by programmers and should be fixed in programs, for example, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and NullPointerException are the most common RuntimeExceptions that can be fixed by modifying the code; this kind of exception is checked at runtime.

1.2. Checked exceptions

Checked exceptions: Any exception that derives from the class Exception except for RuntimeException(Eck, 2019), for instance, FileNotFoundException and IOException are the most common checked exceptions; “checked” means that these exceptions are checked at compile-time; unlike unchecked exceptions, checked exceptions require mandatory handling. In this case, we can add the throws keyword to the method header to throw exceptions for the caller to handle. Or use try…catch… blocks to handle such exceptions directly.

2. The roles responsible for catching and handling different exceptions

There are two roles responsible for exception handling. On the one hand, the programmer can explicitly handle some exceptions by modifying the program. In other words, the computer program is responsible for handling these types of exceptions. On the other hand, there are exceptions that are beyond the developer’s control and cannot be handled explicitly, so the JVM handles them. That is, the computer is responsible for handling these exceptions.

2.1. Error

The computer is responsible for catching and handling exceptions derived from the Error class. This is because exceptions derived from the Error class are usually fatal and beyond one’s control, so programmers should avoid catching or throwing such exceptions in their programs. Instead, let the JVM handle these exceptions.

For example, if there is some illegal data in the compiled Java class, a ClassFormatError will occur (Eck, 2019). However, we cannot catch and handle such errors. Instead, the computer reports an error and handles it when it occurs.

2.2 RuntimeException

The computer program is responsible for catching and handling exceptions derived from the class RuntimeException. This is because RuntimeExceptions are usually caused by programmers and can be fixed in code.

For example, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is a RuntimeException. We can avoid this exception by checking the index before using it. Therefore, the programmer can avoid this exception by modifying the code. In other words, the computer program is responsible for catching and handling RuntimeException.

2.3 Checked exceptions

The computer program is responsible for catching and handling checked exceptions. This is because checked exceptions need to be handled forcibly. Otherwise, the compiler will issue an error message.

For example, FileNotFoundException is a checked exception. So, we need to either use a try…catch… block to handle this exception or throw this exception in the method header.

Codes:

Using try...catch... block to handle exceptions
Adding throws in the method header to handle exceptions

3. In conclusion

The computer (JVM) is responsible for catching and handling exceptions derived from the class Error; the computer program is responsible for catching and handling exceptions derived from the class Exception, including the exceptions derived from the class RuntimeException and all the checked exceptions.

Questions

Why does using ADTs (abstract data types) have advantages for program modularity?

1. Definitions

Before I discuss the advantages of ADTs (Abstract Data Types) for program modularity, it is helpful to explain what ADTs and program modularity mean.

1.1. ADTs (Abstract Data Types)

“This term refers to a set of possible values and a set of operations on those values, without any specification of how the values are to be represented or how the operations are to be implemented” (Eck, 2019, p. 450). For example, the stack is a common abstract data type. It includes push, pop, and isEmpty three operations. But the methods that define these operations are all Public, which means that “these methods can be accessed from within the class, outside the class, within the package, and outside the package” (JavaTpoint, n.d., para. 1). Still, when programmers call these methods, they don’t need to be concerned about how these methods are implemented. In addition, the methods implemented can also be different; for example, both linked list and array can implement stack.

1.2. Program Modularity

“Modular programming is the process of subdividing a computer program into separate sub-programs” (GeeksforGeeks, 2018, para. 3). In java, there are modules, packages, and classes. Modules contain packages, and packages include classes which have variables and methods. Program modularity is helpful to increase the code’s maintainability, reusability, and readability.

2. Advantages

Using ADTs (abstract data types) has three advantages for program modularity. Specifically, they are maintainability, reusability, and readability.
